## Findings

Every finding here is an `observation`: it describes where spend went across the account and makes no savings claim. A Team/Enterprise spend report is a per-person bill summed over the export's range, and supports nothing stronger. Findings are ordered by the spend they describe, largest first.

### E2

**Where spend sits across Claude products**

`observation` - 3 product(s)

Net spend by product: 72% Claude Code ($2,195.87), 24% Chat ($740.90), 3% Cowork ($101.66). This describes where spend went; it does not claim any of it is recoverable.

**Measured: $2,195.87** -- spend observed in the report's net spend column on the largest product, Claude Code

**Recoverable: not claimed.** This figure measures what was spent, not what could be saved.

| product | users | requests | spend | share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | 4 | 29,560 | $2,195.87 | 72% |
| Chat | 4 | 9,174 | $740.90 | 24% |
| Cowork | 1 | 6,900 | $101.66 | 3% |

*Product names are shown exactly as the export writes them; this tool does not classify them.*

**What to do.** Anthropic's Enterprise consumption guide describes Claude Code and Cowork as more token-intensive than chat. Product access can be assigned per group, so a product's share can be steered by who has access to it, not only by how it is used.

**Caveats.**

- A high share on Claude Code is expected where engineers are the main users. It is context, not a verdict.
- The report sums the whole export range, so this cannot show whether the split is stable or shifting.

### E3

**Model mix: where spend sits across frontier, mid and small models**

`observation` - 60% of net spend on frontier models

Net spend by tier: 60% frontier ($1,826.45), 35% mid ($1,077.23), 4% small ($134.75). This check makes no routing claim: whether a request needed a frontier model is a property of the request, which this data never sees. This describes where spend went; it does not claim any of it is recoverable.

**Measured: $1,826.45** -- spend observed in the report's net spend column on models the pricing file classifies as frontier

**Recoverable: not claimed.** This figure measures what was spent, not what could be saved.

| model | tier | spend | share | list $/MTok in / out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| claude-opus-5 | frontier | $1,826.45 | 60% | $5.00 / $25.00 |
| claude-sonnet-5 | mid | $1,077.23 | 35% | $2.00 / $10.00 |
| claude-haiku-4-5 | small | $134.75 | 4% | $1.00 / $5.00 |

*Tiers are this tool's classification, recorded in the pricing file -- not Anthropic's.*

**What to do.** If some usage is simple -- quick questions, short rewrites -- a smaller default model may serve it. Admins can set the organization's default model and restrict which models a group can use. Try a change on one group first; this data cannot say which requests needed a frontier model.

**Caveats.**

- This check cannot tell whether any request needed the model it used. It reports the mix; sizing a change takes per-request evaluation, which a spend report cannot support.
- Published routing research reports large savings at high quality retention: RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2024, arXiv:2406.18665) cut costs "by over 2 times in certain cases" on widely-recognized benchmarks. That was on benchmark prompts, with other vendors' models and a trained router. None of it transfers to this workload without per-request evaluation.
- List prices are the API rate card in the pricing file. Plan pricing may differ; the spend column is what the report says was spent.

### E1

**How concentrated spend is across users**

`observation` - top 1 of 9 users

The top 1 of 9 users account for 25% of net spend ($772.22 of $3,038.43). The median user's net spend was $289.34. This describes where spend went; it does not claim any of it is recoverable.

**Measured: $772.22** -- spend observed in the report's net spend column for the top 1 user(s)

**Recoverable: not claimed.** This figure measures what was spent, not what could be saved.

| user | products | requests | spend | share |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| lena@example.com | Claude Code | 3,220 | $764.89 | 25% |
| eve@example.com | Claude Code | 15,300 | $437.84 | 14% |

*Users ranked by net spend, largest first; at most 10 shown. Share is of the account's total.*

**What to do.** Talk to the heaviest users before changing anything -- they are often the people getting the most out of it. Where usage does need bounding, Team and Enterprise plans support spend limits at the organization, group and individual level.

**Caveats.**

- Heavy use is often the most productive use. A large share on a few people is common and is not, by itself, a sign of waste.
- The report sums the whole export range, so this cannot tell steady daily use from a single burst.
- $6.36 sits on rows with no user recorded. It is in the total but in no one's share.

### E4

**Segments where completion tokens are a large share of tokens**

`observation` - 1 segment(s)

In 1 segment(s), completion tokens are 52% of tokens. On the API rate card, output costs 5x as much as uncached input on these models. These segments' net spend was $101.66 across all token types; the report does not split spend by token type. This describes where spend went; it does not claim any of it is recoverable.

**Measured: $101.66** -- spend observed in the report's net spend column for the segments shown, across all token types

**Recoverable: not claimed.** This figure measures what was spent, not what could be saved.

| product / model | prompt | completion | of tokens | spend |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cowork / claude-haiku-4-5 | 20.5M | 21.8M | 52% | $101.66 |

*Shown because completion tokens are at least 25% of the segment's prompt plus completion tokens.*

**What to do.** Enterprise lets users cap the effort level -- how much thinking Claude applies -- and thinking is billed as output. For groups doing quick lookups a lower default effort may fit; for drafting or code generation, a high output share may simply be the job.

**Caveats.**

- Completion tokens include thinking, which is billed as output. The report does not separate the two, so a high share may be reasoning rather than long answers.
- The export does not document whether prompt tokens include cache reads and writes. If they exclude them, the share shown overstates output relative to everything the model read.
- There is one row per person per model, not per request, so this cannot tell a few long responses from many short ones.
- Some work is legitimately generative: drafting, code generation and translation write more than they read.

## What this data cannot show

Every limitation below applied to *this* dataset. They are listed so the numbers above can be read with the right amount of confidence.

|  | Scope | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Warning | enterprise_spend | CSV schema profile 'enterprise_spend' is marked provisional: Anthropic does not publish every column header of the Team/Enterprise spend report -- only some are named in its documentation, so the header mapping has not been verified against a real export. **Fix:** Run with --explain-schema to see exactly which column mapped to which field, and correct the profile JSON if anything is wrong. |
| Note | - | This is a Team/Enterprise plan spend report. It covers seat-plan usage -- chat, Claude Code and Cowork -- and not Developer Platform API traffic, which has its own Usage and Cost exports. Each row is one person's usage of one model summed across the export's whole date range, so there is no daily or hourly breakdown: spikes, off-hours volume, caching efficiency, batch eligibility and context length cannot be analysed from it. Spend is the report's own figure, not re-priced by this tool. **Fix:** For API traffic, run this tool on a Developer Console export or an Admin API fetch instead. |

## How to check these numbers

Every dollar figure here is the report's own. Model tiers and list prices come from `pricing/2026-10.json`, fetched 2026-10-03; the tiers are this tool's classification and can be edited there. Column names were matched by the `enterprise_spend` schema profile, which is provisional: run with `--explain-schema` to see what each column mapped to.
